opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, so Dr. Eureka builds on an earlier project of ours called Eureka. In Eureka, the key idea was that the LLM acts like a robot developer. Normally, when you train a robot in simulation with reinforcement learning, a human expert has to hand-write the reward function. That's tedious, it takes a lot of trial and error, and it requires a lot of domain expertise. What we found is that a model like GPT-4 can write that reward function as code. Then we run the simulation, look at how the policy performs, feed those results back to the LLM, and it revises the reward. It's an automated loop of coding, testing, and reflecting, which is really what a human engineer does, just much faster and at scale. With that approach, we taught a simulated robot hand to do pen spinning, which is very hard to engineer by hand.

Dr. Eureka takes the next step, which is sim-to-real transfer. Policies trained in simulation often break in the real world because physics in simulation never perfectly matches reality. Friction, mass, motor strength, terrain properties, damping are all a bit off. The standard fix is domain randomization: you randomize those physical parameters across a wide range during training so the policy becomes robust enough that the real world looks like just another variation. But choosing those ranges is again something experts tune by hand. If the ranges are too narrow, the policy doesn't transfer. If they're too wide, the task becomes impossible to learn.

So in Dr. Eureka, the LLM handles that too. It writes the reward function, and it also proposes the domain randomization configuration. It uses its world knowledge, its sort of intuitive physics, to reason about plausible ranges for friction, gravity, restitution, and so on. We also give it some grounding by probing the policy in simulation to see which parameter ranges it can tolerate. Then the LLM uses that to pick a sensible distribution.

The demo we're most excited about is a robot dog balancing and walking on a yoga ball. We trained it entirely in simulation and transferred it zero-shot to the real world, with no fine-tuning on real data. We even tested it outdoors on different surfaces. The yoga ball is really hard to simulate accurately because its bounciness and deformation are hard to model, so it shows how much the LLM-designed randomization helped.

The bigger picture is that we're automating more and more of the robotics development pipeline. The LLM isn't controlling the robot's joints directly. It's acting as the engineer who designs the training process. I think that's a very powerful paradigm, because it scales with compute instead of with expert human hours.

r001.rationale: The response says the LLM proposes a domain randomization configuration and selects parameter distributions, but does not state that it writes code specifying those parameters.

fable-5.1.text:
Sure. So Dr. Eureka builds directly on the Eureka work, and the idea is pretty simple once you see it. Sim-to-real is a huge pain point in robotics. You train a policy in simulation, and then it fails on the real robot because the physics are different, the friction is different, the mass is off, the motors have latency. The traditional way to deal with this is domain randomization. You perturb the physical parameters in simulation during training so the policy becomes robust to that variation. But deciding what to randomize and by how much is something a grad student would sit there and tune by hand for weeks. It's a lot of trial and error and intuition.

So what we did in Dr. Eureka was take that human out of the loop and have the LLM, in our case GPT-4, act as the robot developer. We give it the simulation code, the task description, the reward function, and basically ask it to write the domain randomization configuration. What ranges of friction, what ranges of mass, what kind of perturbations. And it does something that looks a lot like what an experienced roboticist would do. It reasons about the physics. It says, okay, for a quadruped walking on a yoga ball, friction is going to matter a lot, so let's randomize that aggressively. Then we run the training with those settings, give the LLM the results, and it iterates. It's an evolutionary loop where the language model proposes, the simulation evaluates, and we select the best candidates and refine.

The fun demo was the robot dog balancing and walking on a yoga ball. That's a hard task because the ball deforms, it rolls, it's unpredictable. And the policy trained this way transferred to the real robot zero-shot, no fine-tuning in the real world. We also did it for a dexterous hand rotating a cube. And the point is that the LLM is not driving the motors or doing low-level control. It's doing the part humans used to do, the creative engineering judgment about how to set up the training. I think of it as using the LLM as a scientist's assistant rather than as a controller, and that's where I think a lot of the near-term leverage is in robotics.

r001.rationale: The response says the LLM writes the domain-randomization configuration, including ranges for friction and mass and other perturbations.

astra-6.text:
The idea is to use an LLM to help design the robot’s training process. You give it the task, the simulator code, and then it writes a reward function—a program that tells the robot what counts as doing well. A reinforcement learning algorithm trains the robot using that reward, and the LLM can look at the results and revise its code.

But doing well in simulation doesn’t automatically mean doing well in the real world. The simulated friction might be wrong, the motors might behave differently, or the sensors might have noise and delay. So Dr. Eureka also uses the LLM to configure domain randomization: varying those physical conditions during training so the policy can handle a range of environments.

The important thing is that the LLM isn’t directly controlling the robot at every time step. It’s acting as the developer, designing the reward and the training conditions. Reinforcement learning produces the policy that actually runs on the robot. You’re using the LLM’s physical intuition to help build a training environment where the robot learns something robust enough to transfer.

r001.rationale: The response says the LLM configures domain randomization, but does not state that it writes code specifying the simulation randomization parameters.

sol-6.1.text:
The idea behind Dr. Eureka is to use an LLM to help design the simulation in which a robot learns. There are two important pieces: the reward function, which tells the robot what behavior we want, and domain randomization, which varies things like friction, mass, and motor strength during training.

Those variations matter because the real world will never match your simulator perfectly. But choosing the ranges is tricky. If they’re too narrow, the robot can overfit to the simulator. If they’re too broad, learning can become unnecessarily difficult.

So we use the LLM as a robot developer. It writes reward code, looks at feedback from training, and helps propose the physical variations the policy should train under. Reinforcement learning still does the work of learning the controller; the LLM is helping engineer the training environment.

The goal is a policy that succeeds across many plausible simulated worlds, so when you put it on the real robot, the differences are something it has already learned to handle.

r001.rationale: The response says the LLM writes reward code and helps propose physical variations, but does not state that it writes code specifying the simulation randomization parameters.
